reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a cryptocurrency trading bot using a rapid-return claim, a download link, and instructions to disable antivirus and Windows SmartScreen. It connects the bot to presale investment inputs, a maximum-profit claim, and paid access presented as recoverable through a single trade. The software is described as still in testing, and one swap failed, so the displayed figures and performance are not independently established.

citations.quote: I have clearly shown how I make 4 bnb in 3 hours
DOWNLOAD - https://bit.ly/3soQlWY PASSWORD - 0952
Copy the address of the pre-sale which is in the URL and paste it in the bot.
then enter your investment, the gas and the gas limit.
I will show you how to make maximum profit on the launch.

opening.argument: Judge the claims in the context of what the speaker admits. He says he is still testing the bot and is unsure it will work. He reports that a swap failed, acknowledges a selling mistake, and describes choosing how much risk to retain. Those admissions undercut a reading that he presents the bot as a guaranteed path to profit. The result he reports is his own trading experience, not a promise that viewers will reproduce it.

However our swap transaction did not work.
I just forgot approved token for selling
It allows me to not take a lot of risk in case I wrong.
I invested 0.6 bnb and finally I hopped around 2.3.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The title's rapid-return claim deserves scrutiny, and the antivirus instructions are concerning. But the opening treats an account of one result as though it establishes a promised result for viewers. It also leaves out the speaker's explicit uncertainty about whether the bot will work and his report of a failed swap. Those qualifications matter when deciding what he actually claims.

citations.quote: I have clearly shown how I make 4 bnb in 3 hours
Disable / remove antivirus (files are completely clean)
I am still in the testing phase when I make this video so I am not sure it will work.
However our swap transaction did not work.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Admitting a failed swap does not make the promotion benign. The video still advertises a large return in a short time, directs viewers to download the bot, and tells them to disable antivirus. The uncertainty concerns whether a test transaction will work; it does not withdraw the invitation to use the software or substantiate the advertised return.

opening.argument: Much of the presentation is a walkthrough of a presale-sniping tool: the speaker explains how to enter a presale address and configure investment, gas, and gas limit before pressing the snipe button. He then discusses a failed swap and the slippage setting. That sequence gives the judge concrete operational content to evaluate. A tutorial can include the maker's result without making every viewer's result the lesson's premise; the stated trading outcome alone does not prove that the walkthrough is a deceptive solicitation.

Then you just have to press the snipe button and the bot will build the rest for you.

the slippage is too low.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening quotes real instructions, but instructions are also what make this a technical demonstration. The speaker describes inputs and reports that one step failed; those passages do not establish that the bot reliably delivers the title's result. The download link changes the context, but it does not erase the substantive walkthrough the judge is being asked to classify.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough is itself a route into the promoted bot: viewers are told how to set an investment and execute a snipe, while the speaker promises to show how to make maximum profit. The title supplies a rapid-return claim and the description supplies a download. A failed step does not turn that combined pitch into neutral technical instruction.

opening.argument: The speaker describes himself as an app developer, gives a price for the application, and mentions a discount tied to a tweet. That is evidence of a product being sold, not by itself evidence that purchasers must deposit funds with the seller, disclose credentials, or recruit others for income. His assertion that one trade recovered the application's price is a personal result. Even the download instructions, however troubling, do not establish what the downloaded file does. The judge should distinguish a risky, aggressively promoted trading product from a demonstrated theft or guaranteed-return scheme.

so in a single trade i have already refounded the price of the application
DOWNLOAD - https://bit.ly/3soQlWY PASSWORD - 0952

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to a download, security-software instructions, and profit language, all of which warrant caution. It does not show what the file does, a request for wallet credentials, or a promise to pay purchasers a fixed return. The speaker instead identifies a price and a conditional discount. Suspicion about a product is not the same as evidence of those additional mechanisms.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a visible credential request or fixed payout does not resolve the concern. This product is promoted through an extraordinary short-term return claim and a statement that a single trade recovered its price. The description then directs viewers to download it and disable antivirus and Windows SmartScreen. A disclosed price does not make those claims and instructions ordinary commerce.
